summary: Defines two LDAP controls, one in the bind request and one in the response, that let a client ask which authorization identity the server decided to give it after authentication. This helps when the identity differs from the name the client supplied.

plainLanguage.summary: When a program signs in to a directory server with LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), the server may translate the name the client presented into a different directory identity. RFC 3829 defines two controls that let the client ask, as part of the sign-in itself, which identity the server granted, and lets the server answer in the same exchange.

what is the ldap authorization identity control
how do i find my identity after an ldap bind
ldap who am i extended operation
subtitle: Two LDAP bind controls that let a client ask the server which identity it was actually granted.

tldr.problem: After an LDAP bind, the server may map the identity the client presented, such as a certificate subject, to a different directory identity, and the client has no way to learn which identity it received.
tldr.mechanism: The client attaches an Authorization Identity Request Control, which carries no value, to its bind request. On success the server answers with an Authorization Identity Response Control that carries the granted authorization identity.
tldr.outcome: The client sees its granted identity in the bind response, with no extra operation. The controls are not protected by the security layers the bind negotiates, so deployments where the identity is sensitive should protect the channel first.

today: RFC 3829 is an Informational RFC. Nothing in the unit metadata obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the specification of the LDAP Authorization Identity Request and Response Controls.

sections.title: Why a Client Wants to Know Its Identity
sections.content:
RFC 3829 defines two controls for the LDAP bind operation: the Authorization Identity Request Control and the Authorization Identity Response Control. A client sends the first in a bind request; the server may reply with the second in its bind response. The response holds the identity the client was granted.

This matters when the server maps identities during the bind. Client authentication with certificates is the primary case: the subject field of the chosen certificate may not match a directory entry exactly, because the server runs a mapping step. Some Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) mechanisms also omit an explicit distinguished name, or end with an authorization identity that differs from the authentication identity the client supplied. The request control may only be used with LDAP version 3.

A server advertises support for the controls by listing their object identifiers, 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.16 and 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.15, in the supportedControl attribute of its root DSA-specific Entry (DSE).
sections.plainLanguage: During sign-in, a directory server may give you a different identity than the one you presented, for instance when it maps a certificate to a directory entry. These controls let you ask which identity you received as part of the sign-in itself, and the server answers in the same exchange.

sections.title: The Request and Response Controls
sections.content:
The request control MAY be included in any bind request that specifies protocol version 3, in the controls field of the LDAPMessage. Its controlType is 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.16 and its controlValue is absent. In a multi-step bind operation, the client MUST provide the control with each bind request.

The response control MAY appear in any final bind response where the first bind request of the operation carried the request control. Its controlType is 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.15. If the bind succeeded and produced an identity, the controlValue holds the authorization identity (authzId) granted to the requestor. If the bind produced an anonymous association, the controlValue is a string of zero length. If the bind produced more than one authzId, the primary one is returned.

The server includes the response control only when the bind's resultCode is success.
sections.plainLanguage: The request control carries no data, only its identifier. The response control carries the granted identity, or an empty string if you ended up anonymous. It only appears when the bind succeeded.

sections.title: Failure Cases and a Certificate Example
sections.content:
If the server requires confidentiality protections before the control may be used and they are not in place, it returns the confidentialityRequired result code. If the client lacks access rights to the requested authorization information, the server returns the insufficientAccessRights result code.

The RFC's worked example starts with certificate authentication: a client may hold more than one certificate and may not know which one the server selected. The subject distinguished name (DN) in that certificate may not correspond exactly to a DN in the directory, because the server mapped it. After the certificate step, the client can send a SASL bind request using the EXTERNAL mechanism, including the request control. The bind response MAY then carry a response control naming the DN in the server's Directory Information Tree (DIT) that the certificate was mapped to.
sections.plainLanguage: Two refusals exist: the server can demand a protected channel before answering, or refuse because you may not see the authorization information. The main worked example is a client with several certificates learning, after sign-in, exactly which directory entry the server mapped its certificate to.

sections.title: The "Who am I?" Alternative
sections.content:
The LDAP "Who am I?" extended operation provides another way to learn the authorization identity of a bound connection. Because it runs after the bind, a client learns the identity once integrity and confidentiality protections are in place. The RFC notes two drawbacks: the client must coordinate "Who am I?" requests with bind requests and other requests, and learning the identity costs an extra operation.

For multithreaded or high-bandwidth server application environments, the RFC says the bind response approach may be preferable, since the identity arrives without the extra round trip.
sections.plainLanguage: You can also ask "Who am I?" after the sign-in finishes, once the connection is already protected. That costs one extra exchange and needs careful ordering; the controls in this RFC fold the answer into the sign-in response instead.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The controls are subject to the standard LDAP security considerations. They may be passed over a secure channel or an insecure one, and they are not protected by the security layers negotiated by the bind operation.

The response control passes an extra authorization identity, and in some deployments such identities may carry confidential information. The RFC says that in those deployments a security layer should be established before sending a bind request with the request control.

For IANA, the object identifiers 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.16 and 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.15 are reserved for the request and response controls. The request control is registered as an LDAP Protocol Mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer can travel on an unprotected channel, so it can leak the granted identity. If the identity is sensitive, protect the channel first. The two identifier numbers are formally reserved for these controls.

messages.label: Bind response + Response Control
messages.note: Control type 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.15, value is the authzId; only sent when the result is success.
